misconceptions.description: Analyzing a classroom AI decision through only one lens, such as engagement, while ignoring privacy, bias, and policy
misconceptions.trigger: learner recommends adopting or banning a tool after weighing a single factor
misconceptions.feedback: A capstone analysis weighs pedagogy, bias, literacy, privacy, policy, and disclosure together. State how each lens shifts the recommendation, not just the one you find easiest.

misconceptions.description: Giving an all-good or all-bad verdict without naming the tension the decision had to resolve
misconceptions.trigger: learner presents a recommendation with no rejected option or acknowledged cost
misconceptions.feedback: Every defensible decision sacrifices something. Name the strongest opposing consideration and why you decided against it, so a reviewer can audit the tradeoff.

misconceptions.description: Asking the AI tool under review to judge whether it should be adopted, then treating that as evidence
misconceptions.trigger: learner cites the tool's own claims about its fairness or safety as the analysis
misconceptions.feedback: The tool cannot certify itself. Ground the analysis in independent evidence: disaggregated data, the data policy, and your own classroom observation.

misconceptions.description: Producing a balanced description of pros and cons but never committing to a defensible recommendation
misconceptions.trigger: learner lists considerations and stops without a decision or next step
misconceptions.feedback: An analysis studio ends in a committed, justified recommendation with a concrete next step, not an endless on-the-other-hand list.
